title: The に and へ particles
summary: に marks a target of some kind: a destination, a purpose, a place where something is, or what something becomes. へ only copies the destination use.

blocks.text: **に** is a logical particle that marks the **target** of an action. If を is what the action is done to, に is **where it is aimed**. Almost every use of に is a target of some kind.
1. A physical target: where it goes
When you go somewhere, or throw or send something somewhere (or to someone), that place or person takes に.
（私が）公園に行く。 (I) go to the park.

blocks.jp: （私が）さくらにボールを投げた。

blocks.text: 2. A purpose target: why you go

Take the **い-stem** of a verb and mark it with に. This works because the い-stem is a **noun** ("the act of buying"), and logical particles only mark nouns. The place is the physical target; the purpose is the volitional target. One sentence can have both.
（私が）店に卵を買いに行く。 (I) go to the shop to buy eggs.
To be somewhere, you must have got there, so being at a place is a target that has already been reached. に marks the location of existing and being, for people and for things.
（私が）公園にいる。 (I) am in the park. The same に car as 公園に行く; only the engine changed.

blocks.jp: 本はテーブルの上にある。
blocks.en: The book is on the table.

blocks.text: The result of a change is a target too. The picture is transformation: A becomes B, and B takes に. Japanese uses なる far more than English uses "become".
さくらはカエルになった。 Sakura became a frog.
An **い-adjective** cannot take に directly (it is an engine, not a carriage). Change **い → く** to get an adverb, and then use なる: 美しい → 美しく**なる**.

blocks.jp: さくらが美しくなった。

blocks.text: **へ** (read "e" as a particle) is a one-trick pony. It repeats only the **destination** use of に and can never mark where something stays. It also suits a direction of travel, like 北へ (toward the north). So 公園へ行く works, but 公園へいる does not.

blocks.title: Remember
items: **に** marks a **target**: a destination, a purpose, a place where something is, or what something turns into.
い-adjective + なる: **い → く**, then **なる**.
**へ** only marks a **direction of travel**; it cannot mark a location.
